title: A bow, a spade and a basket
hookLine: Lakshmana asks to go, and the text is silent about the wife he leaves behind
tomorrow: why does Rama give everything away?
last: THE RAGE STAYS; HE DOESN'T SPEND IT.

cards: Lakshmana was in the room while Sita won her argument. He heard her say she'd walk ahead of Rama through the thorns.
Now he has his own case to make, and it sounds like a sibling who turns up on moving day unasked and heads straight for the heaviest boxes. It isn't eloquent.
It's practical: who carries what, who walks where, who finds the food. And it ends with a job.

teach.h: WHO WILL CARE FOR OUR MOTHERS?
teach.b: Lakshmana falls at Rama's feet, tears in his eyes, and asks to go. Rama says no at first, with a good reason. Someone must look after our mothers, Kausalya and Sumitra.
The king is consumed by Kaikeyi now. Lakshmana has an answer. Bharata will honor them, and if he doesn't, I'll deal with him.
Kausalya has wealth enough to support a thousand like me. Then the practical part.

teach.h: A BOW, A SPADE AND A BASKET.
teach.b: I'll walk ahead of you with my bow, carrying a spade and a basket. I'll find the path, gather fruit and roots, and do the work, while you and Sita enjoy the mountains. Rama is moved, and says yes.
Then he gives Lakshmana a job: bring the divine bows and armor the god Varuna gave us, kept at our teacher's house.
So the rage that wanted to fight the city becomes a younger brother carrying weapons, a spade and a basket.
Not anger erased, but anger given work.
Hindus have a word for this: seva, service offered as devotion. Lakshmana is remembered as its picture, the brother who walks ahead with the tools.
It's why someone washing pots in a temple kitchen, or serving a festival meal, calls it seva, not chores.

teach.h: AND URMILA? THE TEXT IS SILENT.
teach.b: And here's what the text doesn't say. Lakshmana is married. The day Rama married Sita, he married Sita's sister Urmila.
Valmiki doesn't tell us what Lakshmana said to her, or whether she asked to come. Later poets noticed that silence, and some filled it. Valmiki leaves the space empty.

how: Hindus call service offered as devotion seva, such as washing pots at a temple or serving a festival meal, and Lakshmana is remembered as its picture. Later poets have written about Urmila, whom Valmiki barely mentions.

o: Sumitra's daughter, who goes with Rama to the forest
Kaikeyi's maid, who stays behind to serve Bharata
Lakshmana's wife, Sita's sister, left in Valmiki's silence

games.q: the brother's job — tap the pairs.
p: for digging roots and gathering fruit

s: Valmiki describes Lakshmana's farewell to Urmila
the text is silent about it; later poets filled the gap.
Rama first tells Lakshmana to stay and look after their mothers
Lakshmana answers that Bharata will honor them.
Hindus call service offered as devotion seva
Lakshmana, walking ahead with spade and basket, is remembered as its picture.

games.q: you're Lakshmana. Rama says stay, someone must care for our mothers. what do you answer?
o: Bharata will care for them; let me walk ahead with my bow.
let's take our mothers with us.
games.why: he promises to go ahead with bow, spade and basket, and Rama agrees, sending him for the weapons.

practice: Think of someone whose seva in your life went mostly unspoken: someone who stayed behind, covered for you, kept things running. On each breath in, remember something specific they did.
On each breath out, send them thanks, even silently. Then choose one small act of seva for tomorrow, done for someone without needing it noticed.

wordCard.voice: Urmila, Lakshmana's wife, Sita's sister, married the same day, left in a silence Valmiki never fills. The anger that wanted to fight becomes a brother walking ahead with a bow, a spade and a basket.

orig.note: Sanskrit ūrmilā: the name of Lakshmana's wife, Sita's sister, married on the same day; Valmiki barely mentions her.

carryVoice: Hold on to it: seva, anger turned into service. And somewhere in the palace, Urmila stays. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Valmiki Ramayana, Ayodhya Kanda 31 (Lakshmana asks to go; the spade and basket; the weapons from Varuna)
Valmiki Ramayana, Bala Kanda 73 (Lakshmana marries Urmila)
